overview: The International Nuclear Energy Act aims to help American companies sell nuclear power technology abroad and to offer countries starting nuclear programs an alternative to Russian and Chinese suppliers. It urges the President to create a White House office to coordinate nuclear export policy, and directs the President to launch an outreach initiative and seek financing partnerships with allied countries for exports of reactors and related equipment. The State Department would meet with at least five allied nations on jointly demonstrating advanced reactors, and could give countries new to nuclear power grants of up to $5.5 million (no more than five per country) plus help hiring senior advisors from U.S. nuclear companies, drawing on up to $50 million of existing foreign aid funds over fiscal years 2026 to 2030. It also calls for a recurring international nuclear safety conference, a study of a resource center for advanced reactors, a working group on a strategic investment fund for nuclear and microchip projects, and talks with India on its nuclear liability rules. The law would expire after 20 years. As of June 18, 2025, a Senate committee had approved it and it was placed on the Senate calendar.
for: Supporters say countries building their first nuclear plants are often turning to Russia and China, and that coordinated U.S. financing, training, and diplomacy would help American companies compete while promoting high safety and security standards.
against: Critics say the bill lets the Energy Department waive competition laws and designate specific companies for foreign deals, and that spending foreign aid to promote nuclear exports raises concerns about cost, favoritism, and the spread of nuclear technology.
